facts.fact: Nationalists describe 1857 as India's First War of Independence.
The immediate cause was the greased cartridge of the Enfield rifle.
Mangal Pandey attacked British officers at Barrackpore.
The General Service Enlistment Act 1856 required sepoys to serve overseas.
The Religious Disabilities Act 1850 let converts inherit ancestral property.
Open revolt broke out at Meerut on 10 May 1857.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was proclaimed the leader of the revolt at Delhi.
Kunwar Singh led the revolt at Arrah in Bihar.
Kanpur — Nana Sahib; Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmi Bai.
The revolt spread from Punjab to the Narmada and from Bihar to Rajputana.
The GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule.
The Queen's Proclamation promised non-interference in religion and an end to annexation.
The Peel Commission reorganised the army.
The Indian Councils Act 1861 created the Imperial Legislative Council.
'Ulgulan' was Birsa Munda's rebellion of 1899–1900.
After the Santhal uprising the Santhal Parganas were created.
Indigo declined because synthetic dyes made it unprofitable.
The Andhra region was largely unaffected by the 1857 revolt.
Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy’s uprising is regarded as an early precursor of armed resistance.
Financial decentralisation: Mayo (1870), Lytton (1877), Ripon (1882).
The revolt failed for lack of unified leadership and limited spread.
Scindia of Gwalior, Holkar of Indore and the Nizam stayed loyal to the British.
Sir Hugh Rose defeated Rani Lakshmi Bai.
Bakht Khan, a subedar from Bareilly, led the rebel army at Delhi as its real commander.
John Nicholson led the storming of Delhi and was killed in it (September 1857).
Lieutenant Hodson captured Bahadur Shah at Humayun’s Tomb and shot his sons.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried, exiled to Rangoon and died there in 1862.
Azimullah Khan was Nana Sahib's adviser and envoy at Kanpur.
General Wheeler surrendered Kanpur (June 1857); the Satichaura Ghat and Bibighar killings followed.
Havelock retook Kanpur (July 1857); Colin Campbell finally beat Tatya Tope there (Dec 1857).
Nana Sahib escaped to Nepal and disappeared.
Sir Henry Lawrence was killed defending the Lucknow Residency (July 1857).
Havelock and Outram relieved Lucknow (Sept 1857); Colin Campbell evacuated it (Nov) and retook it (March 1858).
Begum Hazrat Mahal, regent for her son Birjis Qadir, finally took refuge in Nepal.
Sir Hugh Rose captured Jhansi (April 1858).
Rani Lakshmi Bai and Tatya Tope seized Gwalior; she died fighting there on 18 June 1858.
Jhansi was annexed after Dalhousie refused to recognise the Rani's adopted son Damodar Rao.
Tatya Tope was betrayed by Man Singh, captured and hanged at Shivpuri (April 1859).
Maulvi Ahmadullah of Faizabad was killed by the Raja of Powain (1858).
Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur, about 80, fought William Taylor and Vincent Eyre and died in April 1858.
Liaqat Ali led the rising at Allahabad; Colonel James Neill crushed Allahabad and Banaras.
Shah Mal, a Jat zamindar, led the villagers of Baraut pargana (Baghpat, near Meerut).
Maniram Dewan led the conspiracy in Assam and was hanged (1858).
Surendra Sai led the revolt in Sambalpur (Odisha).
Rao Tula Ram led the rising in Rewari (Haryana).
Jaidayal and Haradayal led the revolt at Kota (Rajasthan).
Devi Singh led the rising at Mathura.
Sir Colin Campbell was the Commander-in-Chief who directed the suppression (Anson had died of cholera).
The 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur refused the new cartridges in February 1857.
Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry attacked officers on 29 March 1857 and was hanged on 8 April (the PDF gives 8 April for the attack).
At Meerut the 3rd Light Cavalry sepoys broke out on Sunday 10 May 1857 and reached Delhi on 11 May.
Chapatis and lotus flowers were passed from village to village as symbols before the revolt.
The new rifle was the Enfield P-53, whose cartridge had to be bitten open.
Awadh was annexed on 7 February 1856 and Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was sent to Calcutta; most Bengal sepoys came from Awadh.
The Company stopped the pension of Nana Sahib, adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II.
The Inam Commission (1852) in Bombay confiscated thousands of estates.
Sepoys lost the foreign-service allowance (bhatta) and free postage (Post Office Act 1854).
The British announced that Bahadur Shah's successors would leave the Red Fort and lose the imperial title.
Canning proclaimed peace on 8 July 1858.
V.D. Savarkar called 1857 'The Indian War of Independence' (1909).
R.C. Majumdar held it was 'neither the first, nor national, nor a war of independence'.
S.N. Sen wrote the official centenary history 'Eighteen Fifty-Seven' (1957).
Sir John Seeley called it 'a wholly unpatriotic and selfish Sepoy Mutiny'.
James Outram saw it as a Muslim conspiracy exploiting Hindu grievances.
T.R. Holmes called it a conflict between civilisation and barbarism.
Benjamin Disraeli called it a national rising.
Ashok Mehta called it 'The Great Rebellion' (1946).
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan wrote 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (Causes of the Indian Revolt).
S.B. Chaudhuri wrote 'Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies'.
Karl Marx wrote on 1857 as a national revolt in the New York Daily Tribune.
The GoI Act 1858 was titled 'An Act for the Better Government of India' (2 August 1858).
Lord Stanley was the first Secretary of State for India.
The Act abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors (dual government).
Canning read the Queen's Proclamation at a durbar at Allahabad on 1 November 1858.
The Queen's Proclamation is called the Magna Carta of the Indian people.

facts.fact: The Peel Commission fixed the European:Indian troop ratio at 1:2 in Bengal and 2:5 in Madras and Bombay.
After 1857 the British recruited from 'martial races' (Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pathans) instead of Awadh and Bihar.
The first Indians nominated to the Imperial Legislative Council (1862) were the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.
The Councils Act 1861 gave the Viceroy power to issue ordinances valid for six months.
The 1861 Act restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras (devolution); new councils followed in Bengal (1862), NWP (1886) and Punjab (1897).
The Viceroy received two and a half lakh rupees a year in salary.
The Executive Council created after 1858 had five ordinary members besides the Commander-in-Chief (six by 1918).
Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy was a poligar family scion of Uyyalawada (Kurnool) whose family allowance the British cut.
In July 1846 Narasimha Reddy raided the Koilkuntla treasury.
He was captured and publicly hanged at Koilkuntla on 22 February 1847.
In Hyderabad Turrebaz Khan and Maulvi Allauddin attacked the British Residency on 17 July 1857.
The Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and his minister Salar Jung I kept Hyderabad loyal to the British.
The Raja of Vizianagaram, Vijayarama Raju, died fighting the Company at Padmanabham (1794).
The Koya revolts (1803–1862) in the Godavari tracts were led by Tomma Sora; Raja Anantayyar revived them in 1886.
Chakra Bisoi led the Khond uprisings (1837–56) from Odisha into Srikakulam and Visakhapatnam.
The first Rampa rebellion (1879–80) in the Godavari agency preceded Alluri Sitarama Raju’s Rampa revolt (1922–24).
The Pahariyas of the Rajmahal Hills rose in 1778; their land was declared damni-kol.
The Chuar uprising (1766–1816) in the Jungle Mahal of Midnapore was led by Durjan Singh and Jagannath Singh.
Buddho Bhagat led the Kol rising of 1831 in Chotanagpur.
The Ho and Munda uprisings (1820–37) took place in Singhbhum.
The Santhals had settled the Damin-i-Koh in the Rajmahal hills; their Hul began at Bhognadih on 30 June 1855.
Birsa Munda was called 'Dharti Aba' (father of the earth) and died in Ranchi jail (1900).
The Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) followed the Munda rising.
The Bhils of Khandesh (Western Ghats) rose in 1817–19.
Chittur Singh and Umaji Naik led the Ramosi risings in the Western Ghats.
The Kolis of the Deccan rose in 1829, 1839 and 1844–48 when their forts were dismantled.
Tirath Singh led the Khasi uprising (1829–33) against a road linking the Brahmaputra valley with Sylhet.
Chief Nirang Phidu led the Singpho rebellion in Assam (1843).
Gomdhar Konwar led the Ahom revolt (1828) after the British kept Assam following the First Burmese War.
The Zeliangrong movement (1920s) in Manipur was led by the Zemi, Liangmei and Rongmei tribes.
Majnu Shah, Bhawani Pathak and Debi Chaudhurani led the Sanyasi–Fakir rebellion (1763–1800).
Bankim Chandra's Anandamath (1882) is based on the Sanyasi rebellion.
Pazhassi Raja Kerala Varma, the 'Kerala Simham', fought the Company in Malabar (1793–1805).
Dewan Velu Thampi of Travancore revolted against the subsidiary alliance (1808–09) and killed himself to avoid capture.
Veerapandiya Kattabomman of Panchalankurichi led the first Poligar war (1799) and was hanged.
Bakshi Jagabandhu led the Paika rebellion (1817) in Khurda, Odisha.
Raja Bharmal II led the Kutch rebellion (1816–32).
The Wagheras of Okha Mandal (Baroda) rose in 1818–20.
The Gadkaris, hereditary fort garrisons of Kolhapur, revolted in 1844.
Bhagat Jawahar Mal and Baba Ram Singh led the Kuka (Namdhari) movement; Ram Singh was deported to Rangoon (1872).
Bhukhan Singh, a Chero chief, led the Palamau rising (1800–02).
Strikara Bhanj, zamindar of Gumsur (Ganjam), revolted in 1800; Dora Bisoi held out till 1837.
Titu Mir built a bamboo fort at Narkelberia (1831) in a Wahabi-inspired peasant rising in Bengal.
The Faraizi movement was founded by Haji Shariatullah; his son Dudu Miyan led it against zamindars.
Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli led the Wahabi movement, with Patna as its centre.
Digambar and Bishnu Biswas led the Indigo revolt (1859–60) in Nadia, Bengal.
Dinabandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan (1860) exposed the indigo planters.
The Indigo Commission (1860) ruled that ryots could not be forced to grow indigo.
